transcript.text: Tax Incidence without Elasticity
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-21
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish legal tax assignment from economic burden.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

A tax creates a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive. Legal assignment does not determine who bears the economic burden. Equivalent taxes on buyers or sellers create the same wedge and market outcome. Tax burden depends on market responses, not just who is legally assigned to pay.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a per-unit tax that separates the price buyers pay from the price sellers receive.
Find the new quantity where the vertical gap between demand and supply equals the tax.
The buyer burden is the rise in the buyer price; the seller burden is the fall in the seller price.
Do not infer burden from who sends the tax payment to the government.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to assume that legal tax assignment determines the full economic burden. Tax burden depends on market responses, not just who is legally assigned to pay.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TRACING A TAX WEDGE

The horizontal axis is quantity of movies in thousands and the vertical axis is price of movies. Original demand D0 and supply S0 intersect at point e, quantity 100 thousand and price $10.50. A parallel curve labeled Demand with tax lies $6 below D0. After the buyer-side tax, quantity is 60 thousand. Sellers receive $7.50 at the intersection of supply and demand with tax, while buyers pay $13.50 on the original demand curve at that same quantity. The $6 wedge is split equally relative to the original $10.50 equilibrium price, and quantity falls by 40 thousand.

Before the tax, buyers and sellers trade at $10.50. After the tax is imposed on buyers, the graph shows buyers paying $13.50 while sellers receive $7.50. Each side is $3 away from the original price, so each bears half of the $6 tax even though buyers are legally responsible for remitting it.
CHECK YOURSELF
At the post-tax quantity of 60 thousand movies, what price do sellers receive according to the supply curve?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

Tax Incidence with Elasticity
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-22
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use elasticity to determine and calculate the distribution of tax burdens.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Tax incidence depends on relative elasticity: the less responsive side of the market bears more of the tax burden. That side changes quantity less when the tax alters the price it pays or receives, so more of the tax wedge appears on its side of the market. Legal responsibility for remitting the tax does not determine its economic burden.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The more elastic side can respond more easily, so it bears less of the tax burden.
The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden; identify that side from the market conditions.
A tax on cigarettes causes only a small drop in quantity but a large increase in buyer price.
In one market, demand is much more elastic than supply.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to assume that the more elastic side bears more of a tax. The less elastic side bears more. In this particular worked graph, the price changes show an equal split; do not assume buyers always bear more.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COMPARING TAX BURDENS

The horizontal axis is quantity and the vertical axis is price. A downward-sloping demand curve intersects the original upward-sloping supply curve at price $15 and quantity 100. A parallel curve labeled Supply plus tax lies above supply and intersects demand at price $18 and quantity 80. At quantity 80 the original supply curve is at $12; dashed guides also mark quantities 65, 120, and 150 and prices $10 and $20.

The untaxed equilibrium price is $15. With the tax, buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12, and 80 units are sold. Buyers bear $18 - $15 = $3 per unit, so their total burden is $3 x 80 = $240. Sellers bear the remaining $3 per unit.
CHECK YOURSELF
When demand is less elastic than supply, which side is less able to avoid the tax?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

International Trade: World Prices
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-23
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Interpret International Trade: World Prices.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

A world price lets a small country trade at a price determined outside its domestic market. When the world price is below the domestic no-trade equilibrium price, domestic buyers demand more than domestic firms supply and the country imports the difference. When the world price is above the no-trade price, domestic firms supply more than buyers demand and the country exports the difference. Trade changes domestic production, consumption, and the distribution of surplus.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare the world price with the domestic no-trade equilibrium price.
A world price below the no-trade price makes the country an importer.
A world price above the no-trade price makes the country an exporter.
At the world price, imports equal domestic quantity demanded minus quantity supplied; exports use the reverse difference.
WATCH OUT
Do not use high demand instead of world price comparison. A lower world price creates excess domestic demand that is filled by imports.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING WORLD-PRICE TRADE

The horizontal axis is quantity of avocados and the vertical axis is their price in dollars. Quantity is measured in thousands as printed on the axis. Domestic demand slopes down and domestic supply slopes up, crossing at point A, price $7 and quantity 175 thousand. A horizontal world-price line at $5 crosses supply at 125 thousand and demand at 225 thousand.

The domestic no-trade equilibrium price is $7. When the country opens to free trade at a world price of $5, domestic buyers demand more than domestic firms supply, and imports fill the difference. Because the world price is below the no-trade price, the country is an importer of this good.
CHECK YOURSELF
A student says abundant domestic supply automatically makes a country an exporter. What is missing?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

International Trade: Tariffs
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-24
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze International Trade: Tariffs.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

A tariff is a tax on imported goods that raises the domestic price above the world price. Domestic firms respond by producing more, consumers buy less, and imports fall. Consumers lose surplus, domestic producers gain surplus, and the government collects tariff revenue. The tariff also prevents mutually beneficial trades, creating deadweight loss from excessive domestic production and reduced consumption.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Begin with an importing country whose world price is below the domestic no-trade price.
Add the tariff per unit to the world price to find the tariff-inclusive domestic price.
At that higher price, read domestic quantity demanded and quantity supplied; imports equal their difference.
Tariff revenue equals the tariff per unit multiplied by the number of units imported.
Look for lower consumer surplus, higher producer surplus, government revenue, and deadweight loss from overproduction and underconsumption.
WATCH OUT
Do not treat tariff revenue as full welfare loss. Part of the consumer loss is transferred to producers and government; the production and consumption distortions are net losses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING TARIFF REVENUE

The horizontal axis is quantity of phone cases and the vertical axis is their price in dollars. Quantity is measured in thousands as printed on the axis. Domestic demand slopes down and domestic supply slopes up, crossing at point e, price $8 and quantity 150 thousand. Horizontal lines mark world price $4 and domestic price with tariff $6. At $4, supply is 50 thousand and demand is 250 thousand; at $6, supply is 100 thousand and demand is 200 thousand.

At the $4 world price, domestic quantity demanded is 250 thousand and domestic quantity supplied is 50 thousand, so free-trade imports are 200 thousand. A $2 tariff raises the domestic price to $6; quantity demanded falls to 200 thousand and quantity supplied rises to 100 thousand. Imports fall to 100 thousand, and government tariff revenue is $2 x 100 thousand = $200 thousand.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which two effects create tariff deadweight loss?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

International Trade: Quotas
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-25
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze International Trade: Quotas.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

An import quota directly limits the quantity of a good that may enter the country. A binding quota reduces imports below their free-trade level, raises the domestic price, increases domestic production, and reduces domestic consumption. The price gap between the domestic quota price and the world price creates quota rent. Who receives that rent affects the country's national-surplus result, while the production and consumption distortions create deadweight loss.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Begin with the free-trade outcome at the world price.
A binding import quota limits imports below their free-trade quantity.
The restriction raises domestic price, increases domestic production, and reduces domestic consumption.
The gap between the quota price and world price creates quota rent on each permitted import.
Look for deadweight loss from excessive domestic production and reduced consumption.
WATCH OUT

Do not assume quota rent automatically becomes government revenue. It accrues to whoever holds the import rights; auctioning those rights can transfer the rent to government. The recipient matters for national welfare, while production and consumption distortions create deadweight loss.
WORKED EXAMPLE: QUOTA PRICE AND IMPORTS

The horizontal axis is quantity of phone cases and the vertical axis is their price in dollars. Quantity is measured in thousands as printed on the axis. Domestic demand slopes down and domestic supply slopes up, crossing at price $7 and quantity 175 thousand. Horizontal lines mark world price $3 and domestic price under quota $6. At $3, supply is 75 thousand and demand is 275 thousand; at $6, supply is 150 thousand and demand is 200 thousand.

Before trade, domestic supply and demand intersect at a price of $7. With free trade, buyers can purchase at the $3 world price, which creates imports. The quota limits imports, so the domestic price rises to $6. The difference between the $6 quota price and the $3 world price is $3 per imported unit; that $3 gap is quota rent.
CHECK YOURSELF
A student says equivalent tariffs and quotas remain identical after demand changes. What is the key difference?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

International Trade: Policy and Distribution
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-26
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Evaluate International Trade: Policy and Distribution.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Trade protection redistributes income and usually reduces total surplus, so a policy claim must be evaluated against its costs and alternatives. Security, infant-industry, employment, and bargaining arguments may identify legitimate goals, but each claim requires evidence that the policy can achieve the goal and that a less costly policy is unavailable. Sound analysis separates measurable economic effects from the value judgments used to choose among them.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Security can be legitimate, but the claim still requires evidence and comparison.
Compare the free-trade and quota outcomes.
An infant-industry argument requires a temporary, evidence-based learning mechanism and net benefits.
Efficiency concerns total surplus; equity concerns distribution.
Adjustment goals can be pursued through policies with different efficiency costs.
WATCH OUT

Do not ignore efficiency or distribution evidence. Security can be legitimate, but the claim still requires evidence and comparison. An infant-industry argument requires a temporary, evidence-based learning mechanism and net benefits.
WORKED EXAMPLE: EVALUATING A TRADE-POLICY CLAIM

Suppose protection preserves 1,000 domestic jobs but costs consumers $30 million each year. The positive analysis reports both effects and asks whether less costly policies could assist affected workers. The normative decision then weighs security, distribution, and adjustment goals against the efficiency cost. Saying only that protection 'saves jobs' leaves the consumer cost and alternatives unexamined.
CHECK YOURSELF
What is missing from the claim “protection saves jobs”?
READY?

Suppose protection preserves 1,000 domestic jobs but costs consumers $30 million each year. THE CORE IDEA

Trade protection redistributes income and usually reduces total surplus, so a policy claim must be evaluated against its costs and alternatives. Security, infant-industry, employment, and bargaining arguments may identify legitimate goals, but each claim requires evidence that the policy can achieve the goal and that a less costly policy is unavailable. Sound analysis separates measurable economic effects from the value judgments used to choose among them.
